column4: Goldman Sachs says commodities are ‘underinvested’ with upside potential
column10: [Yahoo Finance anchors discuss a bullish note from Goldman Sachs on commodities.Video TranscriptRACHELLE AKUFFO: Commodities are key again. Goldman Sachs out with a new report calling commodities under-invested. Just as that market continues what the bank says is a supercycle, commodities are set to continue performing well because of supply constraints caused by things like the Russian invasion of Ukraine, even as CapEx or capital expenditure is down historically. So some interesting moves here, clearly taking this long view. Goldman saying that people really aren't thinking about the future right now. They're sort of looking at the present circumstances and not really thinking about investing for the long-term in this space.AKIKO FUJITA: Yeah, commodities the best performing asset class or on track to be the best performing asset class with just a few weeks left in the year. We're talking about a return of 20%. But I'm looking through these notes, Rachelle. I mean, Goldman is calling for a return of 43%, 43% in 2023. Specifically, they point to the economic growth that's set to rebound from China reopening.Of course, that's still a big question mark. It hasn't necessarily gone smoothly, although it's been just a few weeks here, but certainly that would boost demand. That would certainly help things in terms of the commodity side. And then that point that you just made, Rachelle, in terms of an underinvestment in CapEx, Goldman highlighting that specifically that there simply hasn't been that, even as we continue to see divestments from hydrocarbons.So those two key things, I mean, nobody's going to argue with the fact that this was the best performing asset class this year. But you have to wonder, I mean, how many of those factors all line up going into 2023? Obviously, what's happening between Russia and Ukraine still a big question mark. That has been a big reason behind the rally we've seen this year. But still, if you're talking about a 43% return, which is what Goldman is looking at, that's a pretty significant upside we're looking at next year.RACHELLE AKUFFO: And as you mentioned, a very big if when it comes to China's reopening. Every day, we're hearing about new cases and what the demand might look like. This still hasn't happened yet. The policy about changing zero-COVID only just kicked in. We still don't know what it's actually going to look like by this time next year and if China has the ability to get it under control. So I think a lot of countries are sort of looking at this China reopening story. A lot of hopes there, but we still actually don't have a clear picture of what that's going to look like at this point.AKIKO FUJITA: Yeah, I mean, if you're talking about, what, 3% growth this year, and yet, as we were saying earlier this week, potential projection of 5 and 1/2%-- at least, that's the aim going into 2023-- certainly, that would support the case for what Goldman is saying, but as you point out, still a lot of questions about how quickly things ease up and demand picks up over there.]

column4: Oil: $70-$90 range is ‘somewhere we’re going to be’ for first two quarters of 2023, analyst says
column10: [Prosper Trading Academy CEO Scott Bauer joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss predictions for oil prices in 2023, driving factors for energy stocks and commodities, and the outlook for demand.Video TranscriptJARED BLIKRE: Russia threatening to cut oil output by up to 7% or up to 700,000 barrels per day in response to sanctions and price caps placed on Russian oil in response to the country's invasion of Ukraine. Oil trading, we can see that's up about $2.70-- or 2.76% today, up about $2.00 and change. Just closing in on that $80 per barrel price level.Now we have Scott Bauer, CEO of Prosper Training Academy joining us. And, Scott, I was just reeling off the latest price of oil here. We bounced off $70. Now that's basis WTI here. We had-- and I think that was earlier in the month when we were first getting those actual sanctions by Russia pegged-- I guess plowed on, and now we really didn't see much of the way in negative price action from there. In fact, we're up about $8. Just wondering how you're viewing the oil market in response to this latest news.SCOTT BAUER: Yeah, I have been bullish oil ever since we've started dropping below $100 and buying it on every dip, selling it on any sort of rally here. I've had to get stopped out a couple of times, but $70, $71, Jared, that really, to me, is a short-term bottom. When I say short term, I'm saying at least six months.The floor is put in for a number of reasons. First off, that's where, you know, the administration has said we're going to replenish SPR if we get down there. So to me, that is somewhat of a floor.Also, I think there's just still a tremendous amount of tailwinds in the space here. Number one, as it has been for me all year is what's going on in Russia/Ukraine. Number two is what's going on in China, and I believe that we-- the oil market, anyway, has seen the worst-case scenario in terms of demand, in terms of lockdowns, even with the latest, you know, policy that they've talked about with kind of opening back up and people getting COVID. I think we've seen the worst in terms of demand. It's only going to get higher from here.Story continuesSo there are just a bunch of tailwinds, and that $70 number to me, because of the SPR, that absolutely is a floor.JARED BLIKRE: Yes, President Biden talked about buying oil at $70 per barrel for the SPR to replenish it from those-- from the lower levels that it's fallen to.Now you mentioned the double whammy this year, and we were talking about price bottoms. What about a ceiling? What would it take to see a ceiling in terms of the news flow, in terms of price action? What are you thinking about as you think about those upper targets here?SCOTT BAUER: It absolutely would not surprise me to see oil back in the $90s with a nine handle. To break $100, though, I think is going to be a real tough job. I just don't see any scenario other than-- other than some more major geopolitical conflict that we're going to see oil just get to those prices again. And listen, that's not out of the question-- out of the question, unfortunately. That can happen. But I think this range of the low $70s probably to the mid $90s is somewhere we're going to be for, you know, at least the first and second quarter of the year.JARED BLIKRE: All right, and what about natural gas and some of the other elements to the energy sector? We've seen natural gas prices drop off quite precipitously. That has its own supply-and-demand aspects, but maybe you can just comment on that market a little bit.SCOTT BAUER: It absolutely does. And, in fact, if you're looking at what's going on in Russia right now and the news that they announced that they might be pulling back production here, that is really just for crude and oil products. It is not for natural gas.So I know that, especially in Europe, there has been a shortage. But right now, I'm not going to say it's fine, but the natural-gas supply right now is not as dire, if you will, as what we're seeing on the crude side. And again, if we turn back to Russia, 40%-- almost 40% of all of their export revenues are from the oil space, not from natural gas.So natural gas is still flowing. I don't see that we're going to get a major, major spike again, certainly not to where we were. UMG, which I track very closely, is trading right around $15 and 1/2, $16 right now, which is a low we've seen in probably three, four months. That was as high as the mid $30s just a couple months ago. Maybe we see a 15%, 20% pop in natural gas from here just because of this massive selloff that we've had, but I don't think that we're going to get into the crunch like we might get with crude [AUDIO OUT].JARED BLIKRE: Well, we've been talking about the Russian-- I guess the Russian effect on crude-oil supplies. It seems to me when we-- this doesn't-- this hasn't had necessarily bearish price-action consequences when we talk about crude oil this year, and I think part of it comes from the fact that we have dark supplies so that you never see oil taken off the market considerably. You see a market-clearing price. So at some price, somebody is going to take Russian oil off the market.Just wondering, with all the sanctions in place, with all the eyeballs on this, what are the potentials for violations of that next year? What are some of the situations that could evolve that could actually be bearish for the price of energy that might not be factored in right now?SCOTT BAUER: So in all honesty, there's probably violations going on right now, and there will continue [AUDIO OUT] violations going on. Some of that's just going to be-- let's call it glanced over. But we're not going to see, in my opinion, the price get much below $60, which is that price cap there. Maybe we'll see it a little bit. But that is a number that the G-7 came up with to hopefully reduce Russian export revenue but a price high enough to keep it flowing to the market.So yes, there's always, always, you know, some underhanded deals out there. And when you're looking at, really, the four countries that are really still in the market buying Russian oil, you're looking at Bulgaria, China, India, and Turkey. You've got to think that there's [AUDIO OUT] be some violation there.JARED BLIKRE: Yeah, well, I love doing a deep dive on the oil market and the futures markets on the day before Christmas Eve here. Thank you for joining us, Scott Bauer.]

column4: Oil forecasts see prices at $80-96 per barrel next year
column10: [Yahoo Finance’s Ines Ferre joins the Live show to discuss how oil futures are performing in intraday trading as well as the expectations for oil going into 2023.Video TranscriptJULIE HYMAN: It's been a roller coaster ride for oil prices this year in the wake of Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Is this volatility set to bleed into next year? Yahoo Finance's Ines Ferre is here with a look ahead. Hi, Ines.INES FERRE: Hi, Julie. Hard to believe that earlier this year, we saw oil at just above $130 a barrel. Right now, we're looking at WTI around $80 and Brent crude at $83. But where will these oil prices be next year? Well, I asked several analysts, and let's put up a board so you can see some of the projections for 2023.You've got Ed Morse from Citi projecting that Brent crude will average around $80 per barrel, with WTI averaging $75 a barrel. JPMorgan says that Brent will average around $90 a barrel next year. And then you've got OPIS over at Dow Jones that are saying that Brent is going to be anywhere between $95 and $96, with WTI at around 90.Now several factors are assuming this, though. That supply grows with projects in Norway, in Brazil, Argentina, Mexico, US, Canada. Also the successful reopening of China, and also Western nations able to avoid a severe recession because there are many projections of a recession. But if that recession is severe, then, of course, that would impact demand, guys.BRIAN SOZZI: Ines, you're also tracking some supply news from Russia.INES FERRE: Yeah, that's right. Well, Russia now threatening to cut production of around anywhere between 500,000 and 700,000 barrels a day. And that's why you're seeing crude oil today jumping quite a bit. WTI up 3%-- part of the reason Brent crude up 3%. And that's in response to the G7 price cap of those $60 per barrel.And something interesting, though, some data from Bloomberg that was looking at tanker data in the first week that this measure took in effect, as well as the EU maritime ban of Russian imports-- that first week, you had imports total volumes shipped out of Russia down 54%. Now that's only one week. So you can't really go by one week's data. And there are some other factors that are involved here as well.But if this trend continues, then those measures may not be having the intended consequences that you'd want because what the consequences are of those measures is that Russia doesn't have as much money to fund the war.BRIAN SOZZI: Ines Ferre, thanks so much. Appreciate it.]

column4: 7 Stocks That Do Well When Rates Are Rising
column10: [When the latest Nov. jobs report came in hotter than expected, that was essentially the clue for investors to consider stocks to buy ahead of another year of possibly rising rates. Ordinarily, a robust labor market represents cause for celebration. However, in this case, it symbolized a repudiation of the Federal Reserve’s hawkish monetary policy.Stated differently, for all the central bank’s aggressive tightening, it failed to yield significant results. A strong labor market means more dollars chasing after fewer goods. Of course, the Fed wants the opposite circumstance: fewer dollars chasing after more goods. With other central banks adopting similar tightening policies to address inflation, stocks to buy for rising rates offer much relevance.TRVTravelers Companies$188.91ALLAllstate$135.11LOWLowe’s$201.41DDominion Energy$59.84COSTCostco$462.00WHRWhirlpool$141.19TFCTruist Financial$41.71InvestorPlace - Stock Market News, Stock Advice & Trading TipsStocks to Buy: Travelers Companies (TRV)Source: ShutterstockOne of the go-to stocks to buy for rising rates, Travelers Companies (NYSE:TRV) is an American insurance company. Per its public profile, Travelers is the second-largest writer of U.S. commercial property casualty insurance, and the sixth-largest writer of U.S. personal insurance through independent agents. What this all translates to is that the enterprise enjoys inelastic demand.Basically, no matter potential pricing fluctuations or shifting economic dynamics, Travelers will enjoy consistent and predictable demand. Further, the coronavirus pandemic imposed a sharp lesson on the American populace: anything and everything can happen as we realized the world’s a lot smaller than we thought it was. Therefore, people have an even greater incentive to protect themselves.To be fair, some economic forces may be so severe that they may dissuade even the purchase of critical insurance policies. However, such a draconian scenario may be unlikely. Sure enough, bullish investors recognize the realistic thesis undergirding TRV. On a year-to-date basis, shares gained over 19%, almost the exact inverse of the benchmark equities index.Story continuesStocks to Buy: Allstate (ALL)Allstate Insurance officeSource: Jonathan Weiss / Shutterstock.comShould the Fed continue to hit the accelerator on its hawkish monetary policy, your stocks to buy should concentrate on insurance plays such as Allstate (NYSE:ALL). As with Travelers Companies above, Wall Street recognizes the cynical opportunity in ALL stock. Since the start of the year, shares moved up 13%, a very respectable figure given the extraordinary circumstances.Moving forward, investors should keep close tabs on the insurance provider. Essentially, stocks to buy in the insurance field share a direct, linear relationship with benchmark interest rates. As rates move higher, so too does the valuation of insurance-based securities. While it’s not a guaranteed outcome, the relationship is generally dependable.Further, the smart money also recognizes the protective opportunity in ALL stock. While numbers fluctuate quarter to quarter, since the third quarter of 2021, hedge funds dramatically increased their exposure to Allstate. I don’t think that’s a coincidence given the aforementioned linear relationship with rising rates.Stocks to Buy: Lowe’s (LOW)A New Lowe’s Companies, Inc. CEO Could Be Just Enough of a TweakSource: ShutterstockColloquially, Murphy’s Law states that anything that can go wrong will go wrong. Given that this dynamic may rear its ugly head during a recession – which is exactly where the economy might head if rates continue to skyrocket higher – investors ought to focus their stocks to buy on acquiring shares of Lowe’s  (NYSE:LOW). A major home improvement retailer, Lowe’s offers impregnable relevance.Basically, no matter what happens in the economy, people need to repair and renovate their living spaces. Further, your plumbing doesn’t care whether you’re suffering from a recession or not. If the system decides it’s going to fail, it’s going to fail. Therefore, an enterprise like Lowe’s provides some reassurances for embattled consumers.To be fair, LOW stock made good on its ticker name this year, shedding more than 21% YTD. However, an unignorable development exists. Since Q3 2021, the smart money – the hedge funds – began building their position in Lowe’s Companies.Stocks to Buy: Dominion Energy (D)a truck bearing the Dominion Energy logoSource: ying / Shutterstock.comIf you want one of the best stocks to buy for rising interest rates, it’s difficult to ignore Dominion Energy (NYSE:D). To be fair, Dominion won’t immediately attractive conservative investors. Since the beginning of this year, D stock gave up 24% of equity value. In addition, the back half of the year has been rough. During the trailing half-year period, Dominion shed 20%.As if to pour salt on open wounds, TipRanks notes that the power and energy utility firm has a consensus hold rating. This breaks down to two buys, 11 holds and one sell. That’s not exactly an encouraging assessment. Worse yet, hedge funds remain unconvinced about Dominion. Presently, TipRanks states that sentiment among these institutional investors is negative.However, the naysayers seem to be missing the point. Should rates rise, discretionary spending will likely decline because of higher borrowing costs. On the other hand, the essentials – such as utility bills – must be paid no matter what. Thus, D stock enjoys a cynical upside catalyst.Costco (COST)Costco Stock May Be the Market’s Top Recession PickSource: ShutterstockAs I just mentioned, higher interest rates tend to pressure discretionary spending due to higher borrowing costs. In arguably most cases, this circumstance would impugn the upside mobility of retailers. However, Costco (NASDAQ:COST) represents a different breed. It’s not just because it offers consumer staples such as food and water (or other beverages). Rather, it enjoys a higher-income consumer demographic.According to data cited by Business Insider, your typical Costco shopper is younger and generates an income over $100,000. Presumably, such a high average income indicates higher educational attainment and/or owning valuable skills. In other words, the average Costco shopper will be able to absorb higher rates. And she will be able to absorb the side effects of higher rates, such as a recession.In this case, Wall Street analysts get why COST ranks as one of the stocks to buy. Presently, Costco features a moderate buy consensus view with 17 buys, seven holds and most importantly, no sells.Whirlpool (WHR)image of businessman holding a fiery arrow that's heading in an upward trajectorySource: ShutterstockPrior to writing this list of stocks to buy, I had a choice to make. Do I saturate this list with insurance and utility providers or do I get a bit adventurous? Since I’ve already given you the meat and potatoes of rising-rate insulant names, I’ll dedicate the next two slots with speculative market ideas. First up is appliance manufacturer Whirlpool (NYSE:WHR).At first glance, WHR does not appear to be a candidate for stocks to buy. Really, I can understand people think it’s one of the securities to sell. Since the start of the year, WHR dropped a staggering 41% of equity value. Moreover, Wall Street’s best and brightest do in fact peg Whirlpool as a consensus moderate sell.However, if you think three dimensionally, WHR might be a surprising idea for stocks to buy for higher rates. As you know, appliances represent necessities in the modern age. When they break down, it may be more cost-effective to replace them (instead of repairing them).Well, with millions of white-collar workers operating remotely, home appliances collectively received an unexpected workout. Eventually, that wear and tear will catch up, perhaps within 2023.Truist Financial (TFC)hands at desk near laptop computer, with one hand holding a pile of hundred dollar billsSource: shutterstock.com/CC7Generally speaking, I avoided mentioning banks and similar financial institutions for stocks to buy ahead of rising rates. On paper, higher interest rates bode well for banks. After all, they can charge more for their loan packages, improving profitability. However, fewer entities would be willing to borrow money precisely because said rates skyrocketed. Still, I’ll make an exception this case for Truist Financial (NYSE:TFC).Unlike a major multinational banking giant – I won’t mention specific names – Truist concentrates as a regional player. Per its public profile, the company operates 2,781 branches in 15 states and Washington, D.C. Truist is headquartered in Charlotte, North Carolina. Coincidentally, the Tar Heel State features cities that attract plenty of interest from millennials. Stated differently, Truist operates in a region where the money will be spent, not where it was spent.Currently, TipRanks notes that TFC enjoys a moderate buy consensus rating. Among 13 analysts, six of them rate shares a buy while the remaining seven rate it a hold.On the date of publication, Josh Enomoto did not have (either directly or indirectly) any positions in the securities mentioned in this article. The opinions expressed in this article are those of the writer, subject to the InvestorPlace.com Publishing Guidelines.A former senior business analyst for Sony Electronics, Josh Enomoto has helped broker major contracts with Fortune Global 500 companies. Over the past several years, he has delivered unique, critical insights for the investment markets, as well as various other industries including legal, construction management, and healthcare.More From InvestorPlaceBuy This $5 Stock BEFORE This Apple Project Goes LiveThe Best $1 Investment You Can Make TodayEarly Bitcoin Millionaire Reveals His Next Big Crypto Trade “On Air”It doesn’t matter if you have $500 or $5 million. Do this now.The post 7 Stocks That Do Well When Rates Are Rising appeared first on InvestorPlace.]

column4: 17 Biggest Energy Companies in the US
column10: [In this piece, we will take a look at the 17 biggest energy companies in the U.S. For more companies, head on over to 5 Biggest Energy Companies in the U.S. America is one of the world's most industrialized regions, with the largest economy in nominal terms. This also makes it one of the world's largest consumers of electricity, ranking second only to China through 3.9 trillion kilowatt hours (kWh) in 2021. In terms of sources of energy consumption, petroleum and natural gas account for the largest sources and renewable energy ranks in third place. Sector wise, industrial, transportation, and electrical power use are the largest electricity consumers in the U.S., and natural gas is the most widely used production source, according to data from the Energy Information Administration (EIA).Courtesy of some of the best educational institutions in the world, the U.S. is also leading the charge in researching innovative mediums for generating renewable energy. Not only is Tesla, Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA), an American firm, the world's first car maker to successfully mass produce an electric vehicle, but researchers from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) are investigating methods to improve electricity generation through waves and the Sun, as well as new mediums to store electricity. While solar cells are common these days, these materials are unable to tap the vast amounts of energy that the Sun beams down to the Earth. On this front, MIT is searching for materials that are cost effective, scalable, reliable, and efficient at the same time. column4: Dominion Energy Encourages Customers to Conserve Energy
column10: [Extremely Cold Weather Causes High System Demand RICHMOND, Va., Dec. 24, 2022 /PRNewswire/ -- As the evening hours approach and temperatures drop to record lows, Dominion Energy encourages customers in Virginia and North Carolina to help reduce strain on the electric grid by conserving energy.(PRNewsfoto/Dominion Energy)Dominion Energy and other utility companies are experiencing high demand on the electric system that will continue for the next few days. Customers are asked to reduce their energy usage over these next few days to help protect the stability of the electric system.Customers can do several things to reduce their energy use:Set thermostats to 68 degrees or lower.Turn off non-essential internal and external lights.Unplug non-essential appliances and devices.Limit the use of major power-consuming equipment such as dishwashers, washers and dryers.Ensure HVAC vents are open and unobstructed.Dominion Energy also continues to respond to other weather-related outages across the system. The best way to report an outage and track restoration time is through the Dominion Energy mobile app or at DominionEnergy.com.About Dominion Energy About 7 million customers in 15 states energize their homes and businesses with electricity or natural gas from Dominion Energy (NYSE: D), headquartered in Richmond, Va. The company is committed to safely providing reliable, affordable and sustainable energy and to achieving Net Zero emissions by 2050. Please visit DominionEnergy.com to learn more.CisionView original content to download multimedia:https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/dominion-energy-encourages-customers-to-conserve-energy-301709867.htmlSOURCE Dominion Energy]

column4: Oil: $70-$90 range is ‘somewhere we’re going to be’ for first two quarters of 2023, analyst says
column10: [Prosper Trading Academy CEO Scott Bauer joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss predictions for oil prices in 2023, driving factors for energy stocks and commodities, and the outlook for demand.Video TranscriptJARED BLIKRE: Russia threatening to cut oil output by up to 7% or up to 700,000 barrels per day in response to sanctions and price caps placed on Russian oil in response to the country's invasion of Ukraine. Oil trading, we can see that's up about $2.70-- or 2.76% today, up about $2.00 and change. Just closing in on that $80 per barrel price level.Now we have Scott Bauer, CEO of Prosper Training Academy joining us. And, Scott, I was just reeling off the latest price of oil here. We bounced off $70. Now that's basis WTI here. We had-- and I think that was earlier in the month when we were first getting those actual sanctions by Russia pegged-- I guess plowed on, and now we really didn't see much of the way in negative price action from there. In fact, we're up about $8. Just wondering how you're viewing the oil market in response to this latest news.SCOTT BAUER: Yeah, I have been bullish oil ever since we've started dropping below $100 and buying it on every dip, selling it on any sort of rally here. I've had to get stopped out a couple of times, but $70, $71, Jared, that really, to me, is a short-term bottom. When I say short term, I'm saying at least six months.The floor is put in for a number of reasons. First off, that's where, you know, the administration has said we're going to replenish SPR if we get down there. So to me, that is somewhat of a floor.Also, I think there's just still a tremendous amount of tailwinds in the space here. Number one, as it has been for me all year is what's going on in Russia/Ukraine. Number two is what's going on in China, and I believe that we-- the oil market, anyway, has seen the worst-case scenario in terms of demand, in terms of lockdowns, even with the latest, you know, policy that they've talked about with kind of opening back up and people getting COVID. I think we've seen the worst in terms of demand. It's only going to get higher from here.Story continuesSo there are just a bunch of tailwinds, and that $70 number to me, because of the SPR, that absolutely is a floor.JARED BLIKRE: Yes, President Biden talked about buying oil at $70 per barrel for the SPR to replenish it from those-- from the lower levels that it's fallen to.Now you mentioned the double whammy this year, and we were talking about price bottoms. What about a ceiling? What would it take to see a ceiling in terms of the news flow, in terms of price action? What are you thinking about as you think about those upper targets here?SCOTT BAUER: It absolutely would not surprise me to see oil back in the $90s with a nine handle. To break $100, though, I think is going to be a real tough job. I just don't see any scenario other than-- other than some more major geopolitical conflict that we're going to see oil just get to those prices again. And listen, that's not out of the question-- out of the question, unfortunately. That can happen. But I think this range of the low $70s probably to the mid $90s is somewhere we're going to be for, you know, at least the first and second quarter of the year.JARED BLIKRE: All right, and what about natural gas and some of the other elements to the energy sector? We've seen natural gas prices drop off quite precipitously. That has its own supply-and-demand aspects, but maybe you can just comment on that market a little bit.SCOTT BAUER: It absolutely does. And, in fact, if you're looking at what's going on in Russia right now and the news that they announced that they might be pulling back production here, that is really just for crude and oil products. It is not for natural gas.So I know that, especially in Europe, there has been a shortage. But right now, I'm not going to say it's fine, but the natural-gas supply right now is not as dire, if you will, as what we're seeing on the crude side. And again, if we turn back to Russia, 40%-- almost 40% of all of their export revenues are from the oil space, not from natural gas.So natural gas is still flowing. I don't see that we're going to get a major, major spike again, certainly not to where we were. UMG, which I track very closely, is trading right around $15 and 1/2, $16 right now, which is a low we've seen in probably three, four months. That was as high as the mid $30s just a couple months ago. Maybe we see a 15%, 20% pop in natural gas from here just because of this massive selloff that we've had, but I don't think that we're going to get into the crunch like we might get with crude [AUDIO OUT].JARED BLIKRE: Well, we've been talking about the Russian-- I guess the Russian effect on crude-oil supplies. It seems to me when we-- this doesn't-- this hasn't had necessarily bearish price-action consequences when we talk about crude oil this year, and I think part of it comes from the fact that we have dark supplies so that you never see oil taken off the market considerably. You see a market-clearing price. So at some price, somebody is going to take Russian oil off the market.Just wondering, with all the sanctions in place, with all the eyeballs on this, what are the potentials for violations of that next year? What are some of the situations that could evolve that could actually be bearish for the price of energy that might not be factored in right now?SCOTT BAUER: So in all honesty, there's probably violations going on right now, and there will continue [AUDIO OUT] violations going on. Some of that's just going to be-- let's call it glanced over. But we're not going to see, in my opinion, the price get much below $60, which is that price cap there. Maybe we'll see it a little bit. But that is a number that the G-7 came up with to hopefully reduce Russian export revenue but a price high enough to keep it flowing to the market.So yes, there's always, always, you know, some underhanded deals out there. And when you're looking at, really, the four countries that are really still in the market buying Russian oil, you're looking at Bulgaria, China, India, and Turkey. You've got to think that there's [AUDIO OUT] be some violation there.JARED BLIKRE: Yeah, well, I love doing a deep dive on the oil market and the futures markets on the day before Christmas Eve here. Thank you for joining us, Scott Bauer.]

column4: Oil forecasts see prices at $80-96 per barrel next year
column10: [Yahoo Finance’s Ines Ferre joins the Live show to discuss how oil futures are performing in intraday trading as well as the expectations for oil going into 2023.Video TranscriptJULIE HYMAN: It's been a roller coaster ride for oil prices this year in the wake of Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Is this volatility set to bleed into next year? Yahoo Finance's Ines Ferre is here with a look ahead. Hi, Ines.INES FERRE: Hi, Julie. Hard to believe that earlier this year, we saw oil at just above $130 a barrel. Right now, we're looking at WTI around $80 and Brent crude at $83. But where will these oil prices be next year? Well, I asked several analysts, and let's put up a board so you can see some of the projections for 2023.You've got Ed Morse from Citi projecting that Brent crude will average around $80 per barrel, with WTI averaging $75 a barrel. JPMorgan says that Brent will average around $90 a barrel next year. And then you've got OPIS over at Dow Jones that are saying that Brent is going to be anywhere between $95 and $96, with WTI at around 90.Now several factors are assuming this, though. That supply grows with projects in Norway, in Brazil, Argentina, Mexico, US, Canada. Also the successful reopening of China, and also Western nations able to avoid a severe recession because there are many projections of a recession. But if that recession is severe, then, of course, that would impact demand, guys.BRIAN SOZZI: Ines, you're also tracking some supply news from Russia.INES FERRE: Yeah, that's right. Well, Russia now threatening to cut production of around anywhere between 500,000 and 700,000 barrels a day. And that's why you're seeing crude oil today jumping quite a bit. WTI up 3%-- part of the reason Brent crude up 3%. And that's in response to the G7 price cap of those $60 per barrel.And something interesting, though, some data from Bloomberg that was looking at tanker data in the first week that this measure took in effect, as well as the EU maritime ban of Russian imports-- that first week, you had imports total volumes shipped out of Russia down 54%. Now that's only one week. So you can't really go by one week's data. And there are some other factors that are involved here as well.But if this trend continues, then those measures may not be having the intended consequences that you'd want because what the consequences are of those measures is that Russia doesn't have as much money to fund the war.BRIAN SOZZI: Ines Ferre, thanks so much. Appreciate it.]

column4: 7 Stocks That Do Well When Rates Are Rising
column10: [When the latest Nov. jobs report came in hotter than expected, that was essentially the clue for investors to consider stocks to buy ahead of another year of possibly rising rates. Ordinarily, a robust labor market represents cause for celebration. However, in this case, it symbolized a repudiation of the Federal Reserve’s hawkish monetary policy.Stated differently, for all the central bank’s aggressive tightening, it failed to yield significant results. A strong labor market means more dollars chasing after fewer goods. Of course, the Fed wants the opposite circumstance: fewer dollars chasing after more goods. With other central banks adopting similar tightening policies to address inflation, stocks to buy for rising rates offer much relevance.TRVTravelers Companies$188.91ALLAllstate$135.11LOWLowe’s$201.41DDominion Energy$59.84COSTCostco$462.00WHRWhirlpool$141.19TFCTruist Financial$41.71InvestorPlace - Stock Market News, Stock Advice & Trading TipsStocks to Buy: Travelers Companies (TRV)Source: ShutterstockOne of the go-to stocks to buy for rising rates, Travelers Companies (NYSE:TRV) is an American insurance company. Per its public profile, Travelers is the second-largest writer of U.S. commercial property casualty insurance, and the sixth-largest writer of U.S. personal insurance through independent agents. What this all translates to is that the enterprise enjoys inelastic demand.Basically, no matter potential pricing fluctuations or shifting economic dynamics, Travelers will enjoy consistent and predictable demand. Further, the coronavirus pandemic imposed a sharp lesson on the American populace: anything and everything can happen as we realized the world’s a lot smaller than we thought it was. Therefore, people have an even greater incentive to protect themselves.To be fair, some economic forces may be so severe that they may dissuade even the purchase of critical insurance policies. However, such a draconian scenario may be unlikely. Sure enough, bullish investors recognize the realistic thesis undergirding TRV. On a year-to-date basis, shares gained over 19%, almost the exact inverse of the benchmark equities index.Story continuesStocks to Buy: Allstate (ALL)Allstate Insurance officeSource: Jonathan Weiss / Shutterstock.comShould the Fed continue to hit the accelerator on its hawkish monetary policy, your stocks to buy should concentrate on insurance plays such as Allstate (NYSE:ALL). As with Travelers Companies above, Wall Street recognizes the cynical opportunity in ALL stock. Since the start of the year, shares moved up 13%, a very respectable figure given the extraordinary circumstances.Moving forward, investors should keep close tabs on the insurance provider. Essentially, stocks to buy in the insurance field share a direct, linear relationship with benchmark interest rates. As rates move higher, so too does the valuation of insurance-based securities. While it’s not a guaranteed outcome, the relationship is generally dependable.Further, the smart money also recognizes the protective opportunity in ALL stock. While numbers fluctuate quarter to quarter, since the third quarter of 2021, hedge funds dramatically increased their exposure to Allstate. I don’t think that’s a coincidence given the aforementioned linear relationship with rising rates.Stocks to Buy: Lowe’s (LOW)A New Lowe’s Companies, Inc. CEO Could Be Just Enough of a TweakSource: ShutterstockColloquially, Murphy’s Law states that anything that can go wrong will go wrong. Given that this dynamic may rear its ugly head during a recession – which is exactly where the economy might head if rates continue to skyrocket higher – investors ought to focus their stocks to buy on acquiring shares of Lowe’s  (NYSE:LOW). A major home improvement retailer, Lowe’s offers impregnable relevance.Basically, no matter what happens in the economy, people need to repair and renovate their living spaces. Further, your plumbing doesn’t care whether you’re suffering from a recession or not. If the system decides it’s going to fail, it’s going to fail. Therefore, an enterprise like Lowe’s provides some reassurances for embattled consumers.To be fair, LOW stock made good on its ticker name this year, shedding more than 21% YTD. However, an unignorable development exists. Since Q3 2021, the smart money – the hedge funds – began building their position in Lowe’s Companies.Stocks to Buy: Dominion Energy (D)a truck bearing the Dominion Energy logoSource: ying / Shutterstock.comIf you want one of the best stocks to buy for rising interest rates, it’s difficult to ignore Dominion Energy (NYSE:D). To be fair, Dominion won’t immediately attractive conservative investors. Since the beginning of this year, D stock gave up 24% of equity value. In addition, the back half of the year has been rough. During the trailing half-year period, Dominion shed 20%.As if to pour salt on open wounds, TipRanks notes that the power and energy utility firm has a consensus hold rating. This breaks down to two buys, 11 holds and one sell. That’s not exactly an encouraging assessment. Worse yet, hedge funds remain unconvinced about Dominion. Presently, TipRanks states that sentiment among these institutional investors is negative.However, the naysayers seem to be missing the point. Should rates rise, discretionary spending will likely decline because of higher borrowing costs. On the other hand, the essentials – such as utility bills – must be paid no matter what. Thus, D stock enjoys a cynical upside catalyst.Costco (COST)Costco Stock May Be the Market’s Top Recession PickSource: ShutterstockAs I just mentioned, higher interest rates tend to pressure discretionary spending due to higher borrowing costs. In arguably most cases, this circumstance would impugn the upside mobility of retailers. However, Costco (NASDAQ:COST) represents a different breed. It’s not just because it offers consumer staples such as food and water (or other beverages). Rather, it enjoys a higher-income consumer demographic.According to data cited by Business Insider, your typical Costco shopper is younger and generates an income over $100,000. Presumably, such a high average income indicates higher educational attainment and/or owning valuable skills. In other words, the average Costco shopper will be able to absorb higher rates. And she will be able to absorb the side effects of higher rates, such as a recession.In this case, Wall Street analysts get why COST ranks as one of the stocks to buy. Presently, Costco features a moderate buy consensus view with 17 buys, seven holds and most importantly, no sells.Whirlpool (WHR)image of businessman holding a fiery arrow that's heading in an upward trajectorySource: ShutterstockPrior to writing this list of stocks to buy, I had a choice to make. Do I saturate this list with insurance and utility providers or do I get a bit adventurous? Since I’ve already given you the meat and potatoes of rising-rate insulant names, I’ll dedicate the next two slots with speculative market ideas. First up is appliance manufacturer Whirlpool (NYSE:WHR).At first glance, WHR does not appear to be a candidate for stocks to buy. Really, I can understand people think it’s one of the securities to sell. Since the start of the year, WHR dropped a staggering 41% of equity value. Moreover, Wall Street’s best and brightest do in fact peg Whirlpool as a consensus moderate sell.However, if you think three dimensionally, WHR might be a surprising idea for stocks to buy for higher rates. As you know, appliances represent necessities in the modern age. When they break down, it may be more cost-effective to replace them (instead of repairing them).Well, with millions of white-collar workers operating remotely, home appliances collectively received an unexpected workout. Eventually, that wear and tear will catch up, perhaps within 2023.Truist Financial (TFC)hands at desk near laptop computer, with one hand holding a pile of hundred dollar billsSource: shutterstock.com/CC7Generally speaking, I avoided mentioning banks and similar financial institutions for stocks to buy ahead of rising rates. On paper, higher interest rates bode well for banks. After all, they can charge more for their loan packages, improving profitability. However, fewer entities would be willing to borrow money precisely because said rates skyrocketed. Still, I’ll make an exception this case for Truist Financial (NYSE:TFC).Unlike a major multinational banking giant – I won’t mention specific names – Truist concentrates as a regional player. In terms of sources of energy consumption, petroleum and natural gas account for the largest sources and renewable energy ranks in third place. Sector wise, industrial, transportation, and electrical power use are the largest electricity consumers in the U.S., and natural gas is the most widely used production source, according to data from the Energy Information Administration (EIA).Courtesy of some of the best educational institutions in the world, the U.S. is also leading the charge in researching innovative mediums for generating renewable energy. (NASDAQ:TSLA), an American firm, the world's first car maker to successfully mass produce an electric vehicle, but researchers from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) are investigating methods to improve electricity generation through waves and the Sun, as well as new mediums to store electricity. Fusion is the Sun's primary energy source, and all nuclear plants in the world use fission instead. column4: Oil: $70-$90 range is ‘somewhere we’re going to be’ for first two quarters of 2023, analyst says
column10: [Prosper Trading Academy CEO Scott Bauer joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss predictions for oil prices in 2023, driving factors for energy stocks and commodities, and the outlook for demand.Video TranscriptJARED BLIKRE: Russia threatening to cut oil output by up to 7% or up to 700,000 barrels per day in response to sanctions and price caps placed on Russian oil in response to the country's invasion of Ukraine. Oil trading, we can see that's up about $2.70-- or 2.76% today, up about $2.00 and change. Just closing in on that $80 per barrel price level.Now we have Scott Bauer, CEO of Prosper Training Academy joining us. And, Scott, I was just reeling off the latest price of oil here. We bounced off $70. Now that's basis WTI here. We had-- and I think that was earlier in the month when we were first getting those actual sanctions by Russia pegged-- I guess plowed on, and now we really didn't see much of the way in negative price action from there. In fact, we're up about $8. Just wondering how you're viewing the oil market in response to this latest news.SCOTT BAUER: Yeah, I have been bullish oil ever since we've started dropping below $100 and buying it on every dip, selling it on any sort of rally here. I've had to get stopped out a couple of times, but $70, $71, Jared, that really, to me, is a short-term bottom. When I say short term, I'm saying at least six months.The floor is put in for a number of reasons. First off, that's where, you know, the administration has said we're going to replenish SPR if we get down there. So to me, that is somewhat of a floor.Also, I think there's just still a tremendous amount of tailwinds in the space here. Number one, as it has been for me all year is what's going on in Russia/Ukraine. Number two is what's going on in China, and I believe that we-- the oil market, anyway, has seen the worst-case scenario in terms of demand, in terms of lockdowns, even with the latest, you know, policy that they've talked about with kind of opening back up and people getting COVID. I think we've seen the worst in terms of demand. It's only going to get higher from here.Story continuesSo there are just a bunch of tailwinds, and that $70 number to me, because of the SPR, that absolutely is a floor.JARED BLIKRE: Yes, President Biden talked about buying oil at $70 per barrel for the SPR to replenish it from those-- from the lower levels that it's fallen to.Now you mentioned the double whammy this year, and we were talking about price bottoms. What about a ceiling? What would it take to see a ceiling in terms of the news flow, in terms of price action? What are you thinking about as you think about those upper targets here?SCOTT BAUER: It absolutely would not surprise me to see oil back in the $90s with a nine handle. To break $100, though, I think is going to be a real tough job. I just don't see any scenario other than-- other than some more major geopolitical conflict that we're going to see oil just get to those prices again. And listen, that's not out of the question-- out of the question, unfortunately. That can happen. But I think this range of the low $70s probably to the mid $90s is somewhere we're going to be for, you know, at least the first and second quarter of the year.JARED BLIKRE: All right, and what about natural gas and some of the other elements to the energy sector? We've seen natural gas prices drop off quite precipitously. That has its own supply-and-demand aspects, but maybe you can just comment on that market a little bit.SCOTT BAUER: It absolutely does. And, in fact, if you're looking at what's going on in Russia right now and the news that they announced that they might be pulling back production here, that is really just for crude and oil products. It is not for natural gas.So I know that, especially in Europe, there has been a shortage. But right now, I'm not going to say it's fine, but the natural-gas supply right now is not as dire, if you will, as what we're seeing on the crude side. And again, if we turn back to Russia, 40%-- almost 40% of all of their export revenues are from the oil space, not from natural gas.So natural gas is still flowing. I don't see that we're going to get a major, major spike again, certainly not to where we were. UMG, which I track very closely, is trading right around $15 and 1/2, $16 right now, which is a low we've seen in probably three, four months. That was as high as the mid $30s just a couple months ago. Maybe we see a 15%, 20% pop in natural gas from here just because of this massive selloff that we've had, but I don't think that we're going to get into the crunch like we might get with crude [AUDIO OUT].JARED BLIKRE: Well, we've been talking about the Russian-- I guess the Russian effect on crude-oil supplies. It seems to me when we-- this doesn't-- this hasn't had necessarily bearish price-action consequences when we talk about crude oil this year, and I think part of it comes from the fact that we have dark supplies so that you never see oil taken off the market considerably. You see a market-clearing price. So at some price, somebody is going to take Russian oil off the market.Just wondering, with all the sanctions in place, with all the eyeballs on this, what are the potentials for violations of that next year? What are some of the situations that could evolve that could actually be bearish for the price of energy that might not be factored in right now?SCOTT BAUER: So in all honesty, there's probably violations going on right now, and there will continue [AUDIO OUT] violations going on. Some of that's just going to be-- let's call it glanced over. But we're not going to see, in my opinion, the price get much below $60, which is that price cap there. Maybe we'll see it a little bit. But that is a number that the G-7 came up with to hopefully reduce Russian export revenue but a price high enough to keep it flowing to the market.So yes, there's always, always, you know, some underhanded deals out there. And when you're looking at, really, the four countries that are really still in the market buying Russian oil, you're looking at Bulgaria, China, India, and Turkey. You've got to think that there's [AUDIO OUT] be some violation there.JARED BLIKRE: Yeah, well, I love doing a deep dive on the oil market and the futures markets on the day before Christmas Eve here. Thank you for joining us, Scott Bauer.]

Is this volatility set to bleed into next year? Yahoo Finance's Ines Ferre is here with a look ahead. Hi, Ines.INES FERRE: Hi, Julie. Hard to believe that earlier this year, we saw oil at just above $130 a barrel. Right now, we're looking at WTI around $80 and Brent crude at $83. But where will these oil prices be next year? Well, I asked several analysts, and let's put up a board so you can see some of the projections for 2023.You've got Ed Morse from Citi projecting that Brent crude will average around $80 per barrel, with WTI averaging $75 a barrel. JPMorgan says that Brent will average around $90 a barrel next year. And then you've got OPIS over at Dow Jones that are saying that Brent is going to be anywhere between $95 and $96, with WTI at around 90.Now several factors are assuming this, though. That supply grows with projects in Norway, in Brazil, Argentina, Mexico, US, Canada. Also the successful reopening of China, and also Western nations able to avoid a severe recession because there are many projections of a recession. But if that recession is severe, then, of course, that would impact demand, guys.BRIAN SOZZI: Ines, you're also tracking some supply news from Russia.INES FERRE: Yeah, that's right. Well, Russia now threatening to cut production of around anywhere between 500,000 and 700,000 barrels a day. And that's why you're seeing crude oil today jumping quite a bit. WTI up 3%-- part of the reason Brent crude up 3%. And that's in response to the G7 price cap of those $60 per barrel.And something interesting, though, some data from Bloomberg that was looking at tanker data in the first week that this measure took in effect, as well as the EU maritime ban of Russian imports-- that first week, you had imports total volumes shipped out of Russia down 54%. Now that's only one week. So you can't really go by one week's data. And there are some other factors that are involved here as well.But if this trend continues, then those measures may not be having the intended consequences that you'd want because what the consequences are of those measures is that Russia doesn't have as much money to fund the war.BRIAN SOZZI: Ines Ferre, thanks so much. Appreciate it.]

column4: 7 Stocks That Do Well When Rates Are Rising
column10: [When the latest Nov. jobs report came in hotter than expected, that was essentially the clue for investors to consider stocks to buy ahead of another year of possibly rising rates. Ordinarily, a robust labor market represents cause for celebration. However, in this case, it symbolized a repudiation of the Federal Reserve’s hawkish monetary policy.Stated differently, for all the central bank’s aggressive tightening, it failed to yield significant results. A strong labor market means more dollars chasing after fewer goods. Of course, the Fed wants the opposite circumstance: fewer dollars chasing after more goods. With other central banks adopting similar tightening policies to address inflation, stocks to buy for rising rates offer much relevance.TRVTravelers Companies$188.91ALLAllstate$135.11LOWLowe’s$201.41DDominion Energy$59.84COSTCostco$462.00WHRWhirlpool$141.19TFCTruist Financial$41.71InvestorPlace - Stock Market News, Stock Advice & Trading TipsStocks to Buy: Travelers Companies (TRV)Source: ShutterstockOne of the go-to stocks to buy for rising rates, Travelers Companies (NYSE:TRV) is an American insurance company. Per its public profile, Travelers is the second-largest writer of U.S. commercial property casualty insurance, and the sixth-largest writer of U.S. personal insurance through independent agents. What this all translates to is that the enterprise enjoys inelastic demand.Basically, no matter potential pricing fluctuations or shifting economic dynamics, Travelers will enjoy consistent and predictable demand. Further, the coronavirus pandemic imposed a sharp lesson on the American populace: anything and everything can happen as we realized the world’s a lot smaller than we thought it was. Therefore, people have an even greater incentive to protect themselves.To be fair, some economic forces may be so severe that they may dissuade even the purchase of critical insurance policies. However, such a draconian scenario may be unlikely. Sure enough, bullish investors recognize the realistic thesis undergirding TRV. On a year-to-date basis, shares gained over 19%, almost the exact inverse of the benchmark equities index.Story continuesStocks to Buy: Allstate (ALL)Allstate Insurance officeSource: Jonathan Weiss / Shutterstock.comShould the Fed continue to hit the accelerator on its hawkish monetary policy, your stocks to buy should concentrate on insurance plays such as Allstate (NYSE:ALL). As with Travelers Companies above, Wall Street recognizes the cynical opportunity in ALL stock. Since the start of the year, shares moved up 13%, a very respectable figure given the extraordinary circumstances.Moving forward, investors should keep close tabs on the insurance provider. Essentially, stocks to buy in the insurance field share a direct, linear relationship with benchmark interest rates. As rates move higher, so too does the valuation of insurance-based securities. While it’s not a guaranteed outcome, the relationship is generally dependable.Further, the smart money also recognizes the protective opportunity in ALL stock. While numbers fluctuate quarter to quarter, since the third quarter of 2021, hedge funds dramatically increased their exposure to Allstate. I don’t think that’s a coincidence given the aforementioned linear relationship with rising rates.Stocks to Buy: Lowe’s (LOW)A New Lowe’s Companies, Inc. CEO Could Be Just Enough of a TweakSource: ShutterstockColloquially, Murphy’s Law states that anything that can go wrong will go wrong. Given that this dynamic may rear its ugly head during a recession – which is exactly where the economy might head if rates continue to skyrocket higher – investors ought to focus their stocks to buy on acquiring shares of Lowe’s  (NYSE:LOW). A major home improvement retailer, Lowe’s offers impregnable relevance.Basically, no matter what happens in the economy, people need to repair and renovate their living spaces. Further, your plumbing doesn’t care whether you’re suffering from a recession or not. If the system decides it’s going to fail, it’s going to fail. Therefore, an enterprise like Lowe’s provides some reassurances for embattled consumers.To be fair, LOW stock made good on its ticker name this year, shedding more than 21% YTD. However, an unignorable development exists. Since Q3 2021, the smart money – the hedge funds – began building their position in Lowe’s Companies.Stocks to Buy: Dominion Energy (D)a truck bearing the Dominion Energy logoSource: ying / Shutterstock.comIf you want one of the best stocks to buy for rising interest rates, it’s difficult to ignore Dominion Energy (NYSE:D). To be fair, Dominion won’t immediately attractive conservative investors. Since the beginning of this year, D stock gave up 24% of equity value. In addition, the back half of the year has been rough. During the trailing half-year period, Dominion shed 20%.As if to pour salt on open wounds, TipRanks notes that the power and energy utility firm has a consensus hold rating. This breaks down to two buys, 11 holds and one sell. That’s not exactly an encouraging assessment. Worse yet, hedge funds remain unconvinced about Dominion. Presently, TipRanks states that sentiment among these institutional investors is negative.However, the naysayers seem to be missing the point. Should rates rise, discretionary spending will likely decline because of higher borrowing costs. On the other hand, the essentials – such as utility bills – must be paid no matter what. Thus, D stock enjoys a cynical upside catalyst.Costco (COST)Costco Stock May Be the Market’s Top Recession PickSource: ShutterstockAs I just mentioned, higher interest rates tend to pressure discretionary spending due to higher borrowing costs. In arguably most cases, this circumstance would impugn the upside mobility of retailers. However, Costco (NASDAQ:COST) represents a different breed. It’s not just because it offers consumer staples such as food and water (or other beverages). Rather, it enjoys a higher-income consumer demographic.According to data cited by Business Insider, your typical Costco shopper is younger and generates an income over $100,000. Presumably, such a high average income indicates higher educational attainment and/or owning valuable skills. In other words, the average Costco shopper will be able to absorb higher rates. And she will be able to absorb the side effects of higher rates, such as a recession.In this case, Wall Street analysts get why COST ranks as one of the stocks to buy. Presently, Costco features a moderate buy consensus view with 17 buys, seven holds and most importantly, no sells.Whirlpool (WHR)image of businessman holding a fiery arrow that's heading in an upward trajectorySource: ShutterstockPrior to writing this list of stocks to buy, I had a choice to make. Do I saturate this list with insurance and utility providers or do I get a bit adventurous? Since I’ve already given you the meat and potatoes of rising-rate insulant names, I’ll dedicate the next two slots with speculative market ideas. First up is appliance manufacturer Whirlpool (NYSE:WHR).At first glance, WHR does not appear to be a candidate for stocks to buy. Really, I can understand people think it’s one of the securities to sell. Since the start of the year, WHR dropped a staggering 41% of equity value. Moreover, Wall Street’s best and brightest do in fact peg Whirlpool as a consensus moderate sell.However, if you think three dimensionally, WHR might be a surprising idea for stocks to buy for higher rates. As you know, appliances represent necessities in the modern age. When they break down, it may be more cost-effective to replace them (instead of repairing them).Well, with millions of white-collar workers operating remotely, home appliances collectively received an unexpected workout. Eventually, that wear and tear will catch up, perhaps within 2023.Truist Financial (TFC)hands at desk near laptop computer, with one hand holding a pile of hundred dollar billsSource: shutterstock.com/CC7Generally speaking, I avoided mentioning banks and similar financial institutions for stocks to buy ahead of rising rates. On paper, higher interest rates bode well for banks. After all, they can charge more for their loan packages, improving profitability. However, fewer entities would be willing to borrow money precisely because said rates skyrocketed. Still, I’ll make an exception this case for Truist Financial (NYSE:TFC).Unlike a major multinational banking giant – I won’t mention specific names – Truist concentrates as a regional player. Per its public profile, the company operates 2,781 branches in 15 states and Washington, D.C. Truist is headquartered in Charlotte, North Carolina. Coincidentally, the Tar Heel State features cities that attract plenty of interest from millennials. Stated differently, Truist operates in a region where the money will be spent, not where it was spent.Currently, TipRanks notes that TFC enjoys a moderate buy consensus rating. Among 13 analysts, six of them rate shares a buy while the remaining seven rate it a hold.On the date of publication, Josh Enomoto did not have (either directly or indirectly) any positions in the securities mentioned in this article. The opinions expressed in this article are those of the writer, subject to the InvestorPlace.com Publishing Guidelines.A former senior business analyst for Sony Electronics, Josh Enomoto has helped broker major contracts with Fortune Global 500 companies. column10: [In this piece, we will take a look at the 17 biggest energy companies in the U.S. For more companies, head on over to 5 Biggest Energy Companies in the U.S. America is one of the world's most industrialized regions, with the largest economy in nominal terms. This also makes it one of the world's largest consumers of electricity, ranking second only to China through 3.9 trillion kilowatt hours (kWh) in 2021. In terms of sources of energy consumption, petroleum and natural gas account for the largest sources and renewable energy ranks in third place. Sector wise, industrial, transportation, and electrical power use are the largest electricity consumers in the U.S., and natural gas is the most widely used production source, according to data from the Energy Information Administration (EIA).Courtesy of some of the best educational institutions in the world, the U.S. is also leading the charge in researching innovative mediums for generating renewable energy. Not only is Tesla, Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA), an American firm, the world's first car maker to successfully mass produce an electric vehicle, but researchers from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) are investigating methods to improve electricity generation through waves and the Sun, as well as new mediums to store electricity. While solar cells are common these days, these materials are unable to tap the vast amounts of energy that the Sun beams down to the Earth. On this front, MIT is searching for materials that are cost effective, scalable, reliable, and efficient at the same time. To do this, they are utilizing machine learning and rapid experimentation to quickly sift through materials in hopes that a new one will provide a breakthrough.When talking about energy, any discussion would be incomplete without nuclear power plants. There are two kinds of nuclear reactions, fission and fusion. With the former, atoms are split up to squeeze out energy from them. However, the latter is vastly more powerful (and complex) since it requires squeezing the atoms together and the resulting energy is harnessed as power. Fusion is the Sun's primary energy source, and all nuclear plants in the world use fission instead. In the area of fusion, the U.S. federal Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in California was able to generate more energy from a Hydrogen plasma bombarded with lasers than the electricity used in operating the lasers instead.
